criteria.name: The organization has a clearly articulated vision, mission and values understood by employees.

levels.0: No formal vision, mission, or values exist, or the organization is in start-up/pre-operational phase.
levels.1: Vision, mission, and values are documented but not communicated; less than 20% of employees can recall or explain them.
levels.2: Vision, mission, and values are accessible (e.g., intranet, handbook); ~40% of employees can state them but cannot explain application.
levels.3: Regular communication (e.g., annual meeting, posters); ~60% of employees understand and see relevance to daily work
levels.4: Onboarding and performance management reference vision/mission/values; ~80% of employees can give examples of applying values.
levels.5: Values are embedded in decision-making, recognition, and strategy reviews; >90% of employees can articulate and link behaviors to vision/mission; regular employee feedback confirms understanding.

criteria.name: Leadership regularly communicates organizational strategy and priorities.

levels.0: No formal strategy exists (e.g., crisis mode, no strategic plan).
levels.1: Strategy is shared once a year (e.g., annual address) with no follow-up; no documented communication plan.
levels.2: Leaders send occasional emails or hold quarterly meetings; no consistent cadence or two-way dialogue.
levels.3: Monthly/quarterly leader updates occur; strategy is linked to team goals but not always personalized.
levels.4: Multi-channel communication (e.g., town halls, newsletters, team huddles) with clear calendar; employees can state top 3 priorities for their unit.
levels.5: Strategy communication is bidirectional (e.g., leader Q&A, feedback loops); priorities are adapted for each level; real-time updates via digital tools; employee surveys show high clarity on priorities.

criteria.name: Leaders demonstrate ethical and accountable behavior.

levels.0: No code of conduct or ethics policy exists.
levels.1: Code of conduct exists but is not enforced; leaders have been observed violating rules without consequences.
levels.2: Code is published; occasional ethics training; some leaders model accountability but inconsistent.
levels.3: Leaders publicly commit to ethics (e.g., signed pledges); minor accountability lapses are addressed; whistleblower channel exists.
levels.4: Accountability metrics for leaders (e.g., 360° feedback on ethics); transparent reporting of breaches; leaders model 'speak-up' culture.
levels.5: Ethical behavior is a key leadership competency in performance reviews; third-party audits of leader conduct; zero retaliation policy proven; organization recognized externally for ethical leadership.

criteria.name: HR strategy is aligned with overall business strategy.

levels.0: HR operates purely administratively with no strategic plan.
levels.1: HR strategy exists but is unrelated to business goals (e.g., generic talent plan).
levels.2: HR participates in business planning meetings but alignment is ad hoc; some HR initiatives match business needs (e.g., hiring for new product).
levels.3: Annual HR plan explicitly references business strategy; key metrics (e.g., turnover in growth areas) tracked but not yet integrated.
levels.4: HR KPIs (e.g., critical role fill rate, succession pipeline) are directly derived from business strategy; joint business-HR goal setting.
levels.5: HR strategy co-created with business leaders; workforce planning scenarios align with 3–5 year business scenarios; HR metrics reviewed in board-level strategy meetings.

criteria.name: Leadership succession plans exist for critical positions.

levels.0: No critical positions identified; no formal leadership roles defined.
levels.1: Ad hoc replacement thinking (e.g., 'someone could step in') but no documented plan or pool.
levels.2: List of critical positions exists; 1–2 successors named for some roles, but no development plans.
levels.3: Succession plan documented for top 20% of leadership roles; successors have basic development activities (e.g., training).
levels.4: Succession plans for all critical roles (≥50% of leadership); development plans with timelines; annual review by CEO/board.
levels.5: Continuous pipeline with ready-now successors for 80%+ critical roles; simulations/rotations used to prepare successors; diverse slates; measured success rate of internal placements into critical roles (>75%)

criteria.name: Leaders actively promote employee engagement and inclusion.

levels.0: No engagement surveys or inclusion initiatives exist.
levels.1: Leaders acknowledge engagement surveys exist but take no action; inclusion not mentioned.
levels.2: Engagement survey conducted but response rate <50% or no action planning; leaders sponsor one inclusive event/year.
levels.3: Leaders review survey results with teams; action plans created for 1–2 inclusion goals (e.g., flexible work); 60%+ participation.
levels.4: Leaders have engagement & inclusion KPIs (e.g., team climate scores); regular focus groups; ERGs (employee resource groups) sponsored by leaders.
levels.5: Leaders' bonuses tied to engagement/inclusion outcomes; transparent reporting of inclusion metrics; proactive reduction of engagement gaps across demographics; external benchmarking top quartile.

criteria.name: Decision-making structures are transparent and effective.

levels.0: No documented decision rights; employees cannot identify decision-makers for common topics.
levels.1: Decision rights exist on paper but are ignored; employees cannot say who decides what
levels.2: Verbal decision-making process observed but not documented; frequent escalations.
levels.3: Decision making matrix exists for 1–2 processes (e.g., budget, hiring); outdated.
levels.4: Decision rights documented for all major functions (strategy, ops, people); available on intranet; meeting minutes show decisions recorded.
levels.5: Decision logs with rationale (e.g., Confluence, SharePoint); annual review of RACI with process owners; <2 days average escalation time

criteria.name: The organization measures leadership effectiveness.

levels.0: No leadership performance assessment; no criteria defined.
levels.1: Generic manager appraisal form used; no 360°, no team feedback.
levels.2: Annual performance review for leaders uses generic manager criteria; no 360° or team feedback.
levels.3: Annual self-assessment for leaders plus manager rating; no multi-rater input.
levels.4: 360° for all leaders (80%+ completion rate); individual development plans linked to results; team engagement scores used as input.
levels.5: Leadership effectiveness dashboard (retention, productivity, upward feedback, 360° trends) reviewed quarterly; predictive model linking leader scores to business outcomes; external benchmark (e.g., Korn Ferry, DDI).

criteria.name: Our organization's governing or advisory Board regularly assesses the effectiveness of our relations with our stakeholders.

levels.0: No formal stakeholder oversight role exists
levels.1: Stakeholder issues are discussed only when problems arise.
levels.2: Stakeholder relationships are reviewed occasionally and informally.
levels.3: The Board reviews key stakeholder relationships periodically using basic information.
levels.4: The Board conducts regular structured assessments and uses findings to guide decisions.
levels.5: The Board uses comprehensive stakeholder performance metrics, benchmarking, and continuous improvement to strengthen strategic relationships.

criteria.name: Our organization's governing or advisory Board has a formal process of reviewing its own performance

levels.0: No Board self-assessment is conducted.
levels.1: Informal discussions about Board effectiveness occur rarely.
levels.2: A basic self-review process exists but is irregular and undocumented.
levels.3: The Board conducts periodic documented self-assessments and identifies improvement actions.
levels.4: Formal annual evaluations are conducted using clear criteria, with follow-up on agreed actions.
levels.5: Independent and comprehensive evaluations are integrated into Board development, succession planning, and governance excellence.

criteria.name: Our organization promotes agile leadership and management strategies

levels.0: Agile leadership practices are not recognized or applied.
levels.1: Leadership responds slowly and inconsistently to change.
levels.2: Some managers apply adaptive approaches in selected areas.
levels.3: Agile leadership principles are promoted and applied in several functions.
levels.4: Leadership systematically uses agile methods to respond quickly to risks and opportunities.
levels.5: Agile leadership is embedded organization-wide, driving innovation, rapid learning, and sustained strategic adaptability.

criteria.name: The organization's governing or advisory Board is composed of individuals who can provide the expertise it needs and who reflect its values

levels.0: Board composition does not consider expertise or values alignment.
levels.1: Significant gaps exist in competencies and representation.
levels.2: Some relevant expertise is present, but important gaps remain.
levels.3: Board composition generally aligns with required competencies and organizational values.
levels.4: Board membership is systematically selected to ensure balanced expertise, diversity, and values alignment.
levels.5: Board composition is strategically optimized and regularly refreshed to maintain exceptional governance capability and ethical leadership.

criteria.name: The organization's governing or advisory Board regularly evaluates the performance of the organization's chief executive officer using a clear and transparent process

levels.0: No CEO performance evaluation is conducted.
levels.1: CEO performance is discussed informally without defined criteria.
levels.2: A basic evaluation process exists but is irregular or lacks transparency
levels.3: The Board conducts periodic evaluations using agreed objectives and documented feedback.
levels.4: Formal annual evaluations use clear criteria linked to strategy, with development and accountability measures.
levels.5: The Board applies a robust, transparent, evidence-based evaluation process incorporating succession planning and leadership development.

criteria.name: Employees feel respected and valued.

levels.0: No evidence that employee respect and dignity are promoted.
levels.1: Employees frequently report unfair treatment, discrimination or lack of recognition.
levels.2: Some efforts to promote respect exist, but employee experiences are inconsistent across departments.
levels.3: Most employees feel respected and valued, supported by fair treatment and recognition practices.
levels.4: Respect, fairness and appreciation are consistently demonstrated across the organization.
levels.5: A strong culture of mutual respect and employee value is deeply embedded and consistently experienced by all employees.

criteria.name: The organization promotes a positive workplace culture.

levels.0: No initiatives or policies promoting positive workplace culture.
levels.1: Workplace culture is characterized by low morale, conflict or poor relationships.
levels.2: Some culture-building initiatives exist, but implementation and impact are limited
levels.3: The organization promotes teamwork, professionalism and employee wellbeing through regular initiatives.
levels.4: Positive workplace culture is actively reinforced through leadership behavior, policies and employee programs
levels.5: The organization is widely recognized for an inclusive, collaborative and high-performing workplace culture.

criteria.name: Internal communication is transparent and timely.

levels.0: No structured internal communication mechanisms exist.
levels.1: Communication is irregular, unclear or delayed, causing confusion among employees.
levels.2: Basic communication channels exist, but information sharing is inconsistent.
levels.3: Internal communication is generally timely and transparent, with employees receiving relevant updates.
levels.4: Communication processes are well-structured, proactive and encourage two-way interaction.
levels.5: Communication is highly transparent, responsive and trusted, ensuring strong employee alignment and engagement.

criteria.name: Employees can safely provide feedback and raise concerns.

levels.0: No mechanisms exist for employee feedback or reporting concerns.
levels.1: Employees fear retaliation or lack confidence in raising concerns.
levels.2: Some feedback channels exist, but employees use them inconsistently due to limited trust.
levels.3: Employees can raise concerns through formal mechanisms and generally feel safe doing so.
levels.4: Feedback and grievance mechanisms are trusted, confidential and actively supported by management
levels.5: A strong speak-up culture exists where employees confidently share ideas and concerns without fear of retaliation.

criteria.name: Employee engagement surveys are conducted regularly.

levels.0: No employee engagement surveys are conducted.
levels.1: Surveys are conducted rarely and without structured methodology.
levels.2: Surveys are conducted occasionally, but coverage or participation is limited.
levels.3: Employee engagement surveys are conducted periodically using defined processes.
levels.4: Surveys are conducted regularly with strong participation and management commitment.
levels.5: Engagement surveys are institutionalized, data-driven and benchmarked to support continuous organizational improvement.

criteria.name: Survey results are analyzed and improvement actions implemented.

levels.0: Survey results are not analyzed or used.
levels.1: Limited analysis is performed and no meaningful actions are implemented.
levels.2: Some analysis and action planning occur, but follow-up is inconsistent.
levels.3: Survey findings are analyzed and improvement initiatives are implemented for key issues.
levels.4: Action plans are systematically developed, monitored and communicated to employees.
levels.5: Survey insights drive continuous improvement, strategic decisions and measurable enhancement of employee experience.

criteria.name: Managers foster collaboration and teamwork.

levels.0: No emphasis on teamwork or collaboration.
levels.1: Managers operate in silos and teamwork is weak or discouraged.
levels.2: Some collaborative practices exist, but they depend on individual managers.
levels.3: Managers generally encourage teamwork and cross-functional cooperation.
levels.4: Collaboration and teamwork are actively promoted through leadership practices, structures and shared goals.
levels.5: Collaboration is deeply embedded in organizational culture, resulting in strong teamwork, innovation and collective accountability.

criteria.name: Flexible and hybrid work arrangements are supported where appropriate.

levels.0: No flexible work arrangements exist where applicable.
levels.1: Flexible work arrangements are discouraged or inconsistently applied.
levels.2: Limited flexible work options exist for selected employees or departments.
levels.3: Flexible or hybrid work arrangements are moderately supported with basic guidelines.
levels.4: Flexible work arrangements are formally supported with clear policies, tools and management support.
levels.5: Flexible work is fully embedded with advanced policies, technology, and culture; outcomes measured and continuously improved.

criteria.name: Employees feel psychologically safe at work.

levels.0: No initiatives, policies or practices exist to support psychological safety in the workplace.
levels.1: Employees frequently fear speaking up, admitting mistakes or expressing opinions due to fear of blame, retaliation or embarrassment.
levels.2: Some efforts to support respectful communication and employee wellbeing exist, but employees remain hesitant to openly share concerns or ideas.
levels.3: Employees generally feel safe expressing opinions, asking questions and reporting concerns without fear of negative consequences.
levels.4: The organization actively promotes trust, openness and respectful dialogue, with leaders encouraging learning from mistakes and diverse viewpoints.
levels.5: Psychological safety is deeply embedded in organizational culture, where employees confidently speak up, innovate, challenge ideas constructively and collaborate without fear of retaliation or exclusion

criteria.name: Our organization conducts Health Assessment for the development of wellness programs.

levels.0: No health assessments are conducted to inform wellness programs.
levels.1: Health assessments are conducted rarely or informally, with limited employee participation and no clear follow-up actions.
levels.2: Basic health assessments are conducted occasionally, and results are used minimally to guide wellness activities.
levels.3: Regular health assessments are conducted, and findings are used to develop and improve wellness programs.
levels.4: Comprehensive health assessments are systematically conducted, analyzed, and integrated into targeted wellness initiatives with measurable outcomes.
levels.5: Advanced, data-driven health assessment systems are embedded into organizational wellness strategy, enabling proactive, personalized, and continuously improved wellness programs with demonstrated positive impact on employee well-being and organizational performance.

criteria.name: The management allocates sufficient budget to support wellness programmes.

levels.0: No budget is allocated for employee wellness programmes.
levels.1: Minimal or inconsistent funding is provided, limiting wellness activities and programme sustainability.
levels.2: A basic wellness budget exists but is insufficient to meet employee wellness needs effectively.
levels.3: A defined budget is allocated annually to support key wellness programmes and activities.
levels.4: Adequate and consistent funding supports comprehensive wellness initiatives, monitoring, and employee participation.
levels.5: Wellness funding is strategically prioritized and integrated into long-term organizational planning, enabling innovative, data-driven, and high-impact wellness programmes with measurable organizational benefits.

criteria.name: Recruitment processes are fair, transparent and competency-based.

levels.0: No formal recruitment process exists.
levels.1: Recruitment decisions are inconsistent and largely subjective.
levels.2: Basic recruitment procedures exist but are not consistently followed.
levels.3: Recruitment is generally competency-based with documented procedures and interview guidelines.
levels.4: Standardized, transparent and competency-based recruitment is consistently applied across the organization.
levels.5: Recruitment practices are fully competency-driven, audited regularly, technology-supported and benchmarked against best practice standards.

criteria.name: The organization has a strong employer brand strategy.

levels.0: No employer branding activities exist.
levels.1: Employer brand is unclear and inconsistently communicated.
levels.2: Some branding initiatives exist but are informal or reactive.
levels.3: Employer branding strategy is defined and periodically implemented.
levels.4: Employer brand is actively promoted through multiple channels and aligned with organizational values.
levels.5: Employer brand is highly recognized, data-driven, continuously enhanced and attracts top talent competitively.

criteria.name: Diversity considerations are integrated into recruitment.

levels.0: No diversity considerations in recruitment.
levels.1: Limited awareness of diversity and inclusion in hiring practices.
levels.2: Diversity goals exist but implementation is inconsistent.
levels.3: Recruitment processes include some diversity-focused practices and monitoring.
levels.4: Diversity and inclusion are systematically integrated into sourcing, selection and hiring decisions.
levels.5: Recruitment strategy demonstrates measurable diversity outcomes, inclusive practices and industry-leading DEI initiatives.

criteria.name: Candidate experience is measured and improved.

levels.0: Candidate experience is not considered or measured.
levels.1: Feedback from candidates is rarely collected.
levels.2: Basic candidate feedback mechanisms exist but are irregular.
levels.3: Candidate experience is periodically measured and improvements are implemented.
levels.4: Structured candidate experience surveys and improvement actions are consistently applied.
levels.5: Candidate experience is continuously optimized using analytics, benchmarking and proactive engagement strategies.

criteria.name: Digital recruitment platforms are effectively utilized.

levels.0: No digital recruitment platforms are used.
levels.1: Minimal use of digital tools with poor integration.
levels.2: Basic recruitment platforms are used for job postings and applications.
levels.3: Multiple digital recruitment tools are utilized with moderate effectiveness.
levels.4: Integrated digital recruitment systems support sourcing, tracking and communication effectively.
levels.5: Advanced recruitment technologies, automation and analytics are fully optimized to enhance recruitment outcomes.

criteria.name: Time-to-hire and quality-of-hire metrics are monitored.

levels.0: No recruitment metrics are tracked.
levels.1: Metrics are tracked informally or inconsistently.
levels.2: Basic recruitment metrics are monitored occasionally.
levels.3: Time-to-hire and quality-of-hire metrics are regularly tracked and reviewed.
levels.4: Recruitment metrics are analyzed to improve hiring efficiency and effectiveness.
levels.5: Advanced workforce analytics and predictive insights drive continuous recruitment optimization and strategic decision-making.

criteria.name: Graduate, internship or talent pipeline programs exist.

levels.0: No talent pipeline programs exist.
levels.1: Informal or ad hoc internship opportunities exist.
levels.2: Basic graduate or internship programs are established but limited in scope.
levels.3: Structured talent pipeline programs exist with periodic intake and development activities.
levels.4: Well-managed graduate, internship and succession pipeline programs support future workforce needs.
levels.5: Comprehensive talent pipeline strategy is fully integrated with workforce planning, partnerships and long-term talent development objectives.

evidence.name: Candidate surveys
evidence.description: Feedback from candidates on recruitment experience

criteria.name: Employees have documented development plans.

levels.0: No development plan template found on intranet or HR system.
levels.1: Sample of 10 personnel files – 1 or fewer contain a development plan; no update dates.
levels.2: Template available (e.g., Word/SharePoint); HR records show 20% of staff have completed plans; no completion dates.
levels.3: HR system report shows 50% of staff have plans with last review date within 12 months; quality audit shows 70% of those have at least 2 action items.
levels.4: Report shows 80% of staff have plans; manager survey confirms quarterly reviews; sample plans include measurable outcomes (e.g., 'complete certification by Q3').
levels.5: System screenshot shows real-time dashboards; >90% compliance; employee survey confirms plans are useful (e.g., >80% agree 'my plan helps my growth').

criteria.name: Learning programs align with organizational strategy.

levels.0: No learning catalog or training calendar
levels.1: Training catalog available (e.g., safety, harassment) but no link to business plan in documentation.
levels.2: Needs analysis report (dated) shows skill gaps; 1–2 programs (e.g., leadership, CRM) explicitly reference strategic goal.
levels.3: Curriculum map matrix (strategic goal vs. program); 50%+ programs have alignment statement; business leader interviewed confirms connection.
levels.4: L&D budget document shows allocation by strategic pillar (e.g., 40% to innovation upskilling); business strategy document references learning initiatives.
levels.5: Quarterly business review includes L&D impact section; skills taxonomy linked to strategic roadmap; external benchmarking confirms best practice.

criteria.name: Training effectiveness is measured.

levels.0: No evaluation forms, no reports, no post-training data.
levels.1: Sample of reaction forms (e.g., 'rate the instructor') on file; no knowledge or behavior data.
levels.2: Pre/post test scores for 1–2 programs (e.g., compliance, software); no follow-up.
levels.3: 30-day manager survey results for 50%+ of courses; documented behavior change examples.
levels.4: Business result data (e.g., sales lift, error reduction) linked to training cohort vs control group; quarterly effectiveness report presented to HR leadership.
levels.5: ROI calculation sheet (benefit/cost ratio) for 3+ major programs; dashboard tracking Level 1–5 by program type; external validation (e.g., ATD Best Award).

criteria.name: Digital learning platforms are utilized.

levels.0: No digital learning platform (LMS or LXP) exists.
levels.1: LMS exists but is used only for compliance training tracking; <10% of employees log in annually.
levels.2: LMS contains some on-demand content; 10–30% of employees use it; no social or mobile features leveraged.
levels.3: LMS/LXP offers curated learning paths; 30–60% active users (log in quarterly); basic reporting available.
levels.4: Platform integrates with performance management and career development; 60–80% active users; personalized recommendations based on role.
levels.5: AI-driven platform with adaptive learning; gamification, social learning, and mobile offline access; >80% active monthly users; learning analytics used to close skills gaps.

criteria.name: Performance appraisals are conducted consistently.

levels.0: No formal performance appraisal process.
levels.1: Appraisals occur for <30% of employees annually; no standardized form or deadlines.
levels.2: Standard form exists; 30–60% completion rate; deadlines frequently missed.
levels.3: 60–80% completion rate within 45 days of deadline; two-way review process documented.
levels.4: 80–95% completion rate within 30 days of deadline; calibration sessions held for consistency across managers.
levels.5: >95% completion within 15 days; real-time performance documentation (not just annual); automated reminders and manager accountability dashboards.

criteria.name: Employees receive regular feedback and coaching.

levels.0: No feedback or coaching processes.
levels.1: Feedback occurs only during annual appraisals; no coaching.
levels.2: Managers provide ad hoc feedback (e.g., after projects); <30% of employees report receiving quarterly feedback.
levels.3: Quarterly check-ins expected; 30–60% of employees report feedback at least quarterly; some managers trained in coaching.
levels.4: 60–80% of employees report feedback at least monthly; coaching training for all managers; upward feedback on coaching quality.
levels.5: >80% of employees report weekly/biweekly meaningful feedback; coaching culture measured via survey; coaching certifications or external coaches for leaders.

criteria.name: High-potential employees are identified and developed.

levels.0: No HiPo identification process.
levels.1: Informal HiPo list held by senior leader (subjective); no development.
levels.2: Criteria defined (e.g., performance + potential matrix); HiPos identified (<10% of population); minimal development (e.g., one-off mentoring).
levels.3: Formal HiPo pool (10–15% of employees); annual development plan; exposure to senior leaders (e.g., projects, shadowing).
levels.4: HiPo program with curriculum, sponsorship, and rotations; retention tracking; 50%+ of open leadership roles filled from HiPo pool.
levels.5: Differentiated HiPo tracks (e.g., early career, mid-level, executive); predictive assessment tools; 80% retention of HiPos; external benchmark for HiPo development.

criteria.name: Internal promotion and career mobility are encouraged.

levels.0: No internal job posting or mobility policy.
levels.1: Internal candidates rarely considered (<10% of vacancies filled internally).
levels.2: Internal job board exists; 10–25% of vacancies filled internally; no formal career paths.
levels.3: 25–40% internal fill rate; career path documentation for key roles; employees encouraged to apply.
levels.4: 40–60% internal fill rate; rotational assignments or cross-functional moves; internal mobility metrics tracked.
levels.5: >60% internal fill rate; 'internal first' policy (post internally 2 weeks before external); career mobility part of manager KPIs; alumni rehire program.

criteria.name: Leadership development programs exist.

levels.0: No leadership development offering.
levels.1: One-off training for new managers (e.g., 1-day course); no follow-up.
levels.2: Program for frontline leaders exists; <30% of leaders attend annually; no evaluation.
levels.3: Multi-module program (e.g., 6 sessions) for mid-level leaders; 30–60% participation; basic feedback collected.
levels.4: Differentiated programs (emerging, mid, executive); 60–80% participation; 360° pre/post; business impact measured.
levels.5: Leadership academy with certification; executive coaching embedded; 80%+ participation; succession pipeline feed from program; external accreditation.

criteria.name: A system is developed to support and reward employees who take initiatives to develop their skills and professions (skills-based incentives).

levels.0: No system exists to recognize or reward employee skills development initiatives.
levels.1: Informal encouragement for skills development exists, but no structured incentives or recognition mechanisms are in place.
levels.2: Basic incentives or recognition programs are introduced for selected training or certifications, with limited participation and monitoring.
levels.3: A formal skills-based incentive system exists, linking employee learning initiatives to recognition, rewards, or career development opportunities.
levels.4: Skills development incentives are consistently implemented, monitored, and aligned with organizational competency and performance goals. Employees are actively encouraged to pursue professional growth.
levels.5: A comprehensive and innovative skills-based incentive system is embedded into organizational culture, integrating continuous learning, career progression, succession planning, and measurable business impact. Employees are proactively rewarded for upskilling, innovation, and professional excellence.

criteria.name: Compensation structures are fair and competitive.

levels.0: No compensation structure exists.
levels.1: Pay decisions are inconsistent and non-transparent.
levels.2: Basic salary structures exist but are rarely benchmarked.
levels.3: Compensation structures are standardized and periodically reviewed.
levels.4: Compensation is benchmarked regularly against market data and applied fairly.
levels.5: Compensation strategy is highly competitive, transparent, data-driven, and linked to retention and performance outcomes.

criteria.name: Employee benefits support well-being and work-life balance.

levels.0: No employee benefits provided beyond legal minimums.
levels.1: Limited benefits with little relevance to employee well-being.
levels.2: Some benefits exist but are inconsistently applied or poorly communicated.
levels.3: Benefits support basic work-life balance needs and are accessible to most employees.
levels.4: Comprehensive benefits programs support physical, social, and family well-being.
levels.5: Innovative and flexible benefits programs are regularly improved based on employee feedback and industry best practice.

criteria.name: Wellness initiatives are implemented and monitored.

levels.0: No wellness initiatives exist.
levels.1: Ad hoc wellness activities occur without structure or monitoring.
levels.2: Basic wellness initiatives exist but participation and impact are not tracked.
levels.3: Wellness programs are implemented and periodically monitored.
levels.4: Wellness initiatives are structured, regularly evaluated, and aligned with employee needs.
levels.5: Wellness strategy is embedded in organizational culture with measurable positive outcomes and continuous improvement.

criteria.name: Employee turnover is analyzed and addressed.

levels.0: Turnover data is not collected.
levels.1: Turnover is noticed only when problems arise.
levels.2: Basic turnover statistics are collected with limited analysis.
levels.3: Turnover trends are analyzed periodically and corrective actions are sometimes taken.
levels.4: Turnover drivers are systematically analyzed and mitigation strategies implemented
levels.5: Predictive workforce analytics and proactive retention strategies significantly reduce avoidable turnover.

criteria.name: Recognition programs reward strong performance.

levels.0: No recognition programs exist.
levels.1: Recognition is informal, inconsistent, or biased.
levels.2: Some recognition mechanisms exist but are limited in reach or impact.
levels.3: Formal recognition programs exist and are applied periodically.
levels.4: Recognition programs are structured, transparent, and linked to performance outcomes.
levels.5: Recognition culture is embedded organization-wide with innovative, inclusive, and highly valued reward systems.

criteria.name: Mental health support programs exist.

levels.0: No mental health support is available.
levels.1: Minimal awareness of mental health issues with no formal support.
levels.2: Limited mental health support services or awareness initiatives exist.
levels.3: Mental health programs and support channels are available to employees.
levels.4: Comprehensive mental health support services are accessible, promoted, and monitored.
levels.5: Mental health and psychological safety are strategically prioritized with measurable impact on employee well-being.

criteria.name: Absenteeism and retention metrics are monitored.

levels.0: No absenteeism or retention data is tracked.
levels.1: Data is tracked inconsistently and rarely analyzed.
levels.2: Basic absenteeism and retention reports are produced occasionally.
levels.3: Metrics are monitored regularly and trends reviewed by management.
levels.4: Data is analyzed systematically with interventions developed to address issues.
levels.5: Advanced workforce analytics are used proactively to predict and improve attendance and retention outcomes.

criteria.name: Employees perceive rewards as equitable.

levels.0: No assessment of employee perceptions exists.
levels.1: Employees frequently express concerns about unfair rewards.
levels.2: Limited feedback mechanisms exist regarding reward fairness.
levels.3: Employee perceptions are periodically assessed and some improvements made.
levels.4: Most employees perceive rewards as fair, transparent, and performance-based.
levels.5: Reward systems are widely trusted, evidence-based, and continuously refined through employee engagement and benchmarking.

criteria.name: The organization has a formal DEI strategy.

levels.0: No DEI strategy or recognition of DEI priorities.
levels.1: Informal or ad hoc DEI efforts with no documented strategy.
levels.2: Draft DEI strategy exists but lacks clear objectives, ownership, or implementation plans.
levels.3: Formal DEI strategy approved with defined objectives and some implementation activities.
levels.4: Comprehensive DEI strategy aligned with organizational goals, monitored regularly.
levels.5: DEI strategy is fully embedded into organizational culture, operations, and long-term planning with measurable impact demonstrated.

criteria.name: Leadership demonstrates commitment to DEI.

levels.0: Leadership shows no visible support for DEI.
levels.1: DEI commitment is rarely communicated or demonstrated by leadership.
levels.2: Some leaders advocate for DEI, but commitment is inconsistent.
levels.3: Leadership communicates support for DEI and participates in selected initiatives.
levels.4: Leadership actively champions DEI through decisions, accountability, and resource allocation.
levels.5: Leadership models inclusive behavior consistently and drives DEI as a strategic organizational priority.

criteria.name: Gender equity targets and metrics are monitored.

levels.0: No gender equity targets or metrics exist.
levels.1: Limited awareness of gender disparities with no monitoring system.
levels.2: Basic gender data is collected occasionally but not analyzed systematically.
levels.3: Gender equity targets are established and monitored periodically.
levels.4: Gender representation, pay equity, and advancement metrics are tracked and acted upon regularly.
levels.5: Advanced gender equity analytics drive strategic decisions, with continuous improvement and transparent reporting.

criteria.name: Persons with disabilities are supported and accommodated.

levels.0: No disability support or accommodations provided.
levels.1: Accommodations are only provided reactively and inconsistently.
levels.2: Some accessibility measures exist but are limited in scope.
levels.3: Standard accommodation procedures and accessibility measures are implemented.
levels.4: Workplace systems, facilities, and processes are inclusive and accessible for persons with disabilities.
levels.5: Disability inclusion is proactively integrated into organizational design, culture, recruitment, and career development.

criteria.name: Equal opportunity policies are implemented effectively.

levels.0: No equal opportunity policies exist.
levels.1: Policies exist but are poorly communicated or inconsistently applied.
levels.2: Policies are communicated but enforcement is limited.
levels.3: Equal opportunity policies are implemented with basic monitoring mechanisms.
levels.4: Policies are consistently applied, monitored, and supported through training and accountability.
levels.5: Equal opportunity principles are fully embedded, regularly reviewed, and recognized as best practice.

criteria.name: Diversity metrics are reported regularly.

levels.0: No diversity data is collected or reported.
levels.1: Diversity data collection is irregular and incomplete.
levels.2: Basic diversity metrics are gathered but reporting is limited.
levels.3: Diversity metrics are reported periodically to management.
levels.4: Comprehensive diversity reporting is conducted regularly with trend analysis and action plans.
levels.5: Real-time or advanced diversity analytics inform strategic decisions and are transparently shared across stakeholders.

criteria.name: Bias mitigation training is conducted.

levels.0: No bias awareness or mitigation training provided.
levels.1: Training occurs rarely or only after incidents.
levels.2: Basic bias awareness sessions are conducted for limited groups.
levels.3: Regular bias mitigation training is provided for employees and managers.
levels.4: Comprehensive, role-specific training programs are implemented and evaluated for effectiveness.
levels.5: Continuous bias mitigation learning is embedded into organizational development, leadership, and decision-making processes.

criteria.name: Employees feel included regardless of background.

levels.0: Employees frequently report exclusion or discrimination.
levels.1: Inclusion concerns are common and rarely addressed.
levels.2: Some inclusion initiatives exist, but employee experience is inconsistent.
levels.3: Most employees report a generally inclusive work environment.
levels.4: Employees across diverse backgrounds consistently feel respected, valued, and included.
levels.5: Inclusion is deeply embedded in organizational culture, with high belonging, engagement, and psychological safety across all groups.

criteria.name: The organization measures environmental impact.

levels.0: No environmental impact measurement exists.
levels.1: Environmental impacts are rarely measured and data is incomplete or unreliable.
levels.2: Basic environmental measurements exist for selected activities, but monitoring is inconsistent.
levels.3: Environmental impacts such as energy use, waste or emissions are periodically measured and reported.
levels.4: Comprehensive environmental measurement systems exist with regular monitoring and management review.
levels.5: Environmental impact measurement is fully integrated, data-driven and benchmarked against international best practices and standards.

criteria.name: Sustainability targets exist and are monitored.

levels.0: No sustainability targets exist.
levels.1: Sustainability goals are informal, unclear or not monitored.
levels.2: Some sustainability targets exist, but monitoring and accountability are limited.
levels.3: Defined sustainability targets are monitored periodically with management oversight.
levels.4: Sustainability targets are measurable, regularly reviewed and linked to operational performance.
levels.5: Ambitious science-based sustainability targets are integrated into strategy, continuously monitored and publicly reported.

criteria.name: Energy, waste and resource efficiency initiatives are implemented.

levels.0: No efficiency initiatives exist.
levels.1: Limited or ad hoc initiatives exist with minimal impact.
levels.2: Basic initiatives exist for energy saving, waste reduction or resource efficiency.
levels.3: Several efficiency programs are implemented with moderate measurable improvements.
levels.4: Organization-wide efficiency initiatives are actively managed and produce significant measurable outcomes.
levels.5: Resource efficiency and circular economy principles are embedded across operations, innovation and supply chains

criteria.name: Greenhouse gas emissions and Climate-related risks are assessed.

levels.0: No assessment of greenhouse gas emissions or climate-related risks exists.
levels.1: Green house gas emission or Climate risks are recognized informally but not assessed systematically.
levels.2: Initial greenhouse gas emission or climate risk assessments are conducted for selected operations or projects.
levels.3: greenhouse gas emission or Climate-related risks are periodically assessed and considered in planning processes.
levels.4: greenhouse gas emission or Climate risks are systematically assessed, monitored and integrated into risk management frameworks.
levels.5: Advanced greenhouse gas emission or climate resilience and adaptation strategies are fully integrated into organizational strategy and decision-making.

criteria.name: Community investment and CSR programs exist.

levels.0: No community investment or CSR initiatives exist.
levels.1: CSR activities are occasional and unstructured.
levels.2: Some community or CSR programs exist, but impact measurement is limited.
levels.3: Structured CSR and community investment programs are implemented with defined objectives.
levels.4: CSR initiatives are aligned with community needs and organizational strategy, with measurable outcomes.
levels.5: Community investment and social impact programs create sustainable long-term value and strong stakeholder partnerships.

criteria.name: Human rights and labor standards are respected across operations.

levels.0: No policies or practices addressing human rights and labor standards exist.
levels.1: Frequent concerns or violations relating to labor rights or working conditions exist.
levels.2: Basic compliance with labor laws exists, but implementation is inconsistent.
levels.3: Human rights and labor standards are generally respected with supporting policies and procedures.
levels.4: Strong systems exist to protect labor rights, promote fair treatment and monitor compliance across operations.
levels.5: Human rights and labor standards are embedded throughout operations and value chains, exceeding regulatory expectations and reflecting global best practices.

criteria.name: Supplier sustainability expectations exist.

levels.0: No sustainability expectations for suppliers exist.
levels.1: Supplier sustainability issues are rarely considered.
levels.2: Basic sustainability requirements exist for selected suppliers.
levels.3: Supplier sustainability expectations are documented and communicated to suppliers.
levels.4: Supplier sustainability performance is monitored and incorporated into procurement decisions.
levels.5: Suppliers are actively engaged on ESG improvement, with strong sustainability standards integrated throughout the supply chain.

criteria.name: ESG oversight exists at leadership or board level.

levels.0: No ESG oversight exists.
levels.1: ESG responsibilities are unclear or informal.
levels.2: ESG oversight exists at management level but is limited in scope.
levels.3: Leadership or board committees periodically review ESG matters.
levels.4: ESG oversight is formally integrated into leadership and board governance structures.
levels.5: ESG governance is fully embedded at board and executive level with clear accountability, expertise and strategic integration.

criteria.name: ESG reporting and disclosure practices are implemented.

levels.0: No ESG reporting or disclosure exists.
levels.1: ESG disclosures are minimal, inconsistent or reactive.
levels.2: Basic ESG information is reported internally or externally on a limited basis.
levels.3: ESG reporting is conducted periodically using defined frameworks or indicators.
levels.4: Comprehensive ESG reporting and disclosure practices are implemented and regularly reviewed.
levels.5: ESG reporting is transparent, externally benchmarked and aligned with recognized international reporting standards.

criteria.name: Ethical conduct and anti-corruption controls are effective

levels.0: No ethics or anti-corruption controls exist.
levels.1: Weak ethics culture and ineffective anti-corruption controls are evident.
levels.2: Basic ethics policies and controls exist, but enforcement is inconsistent.
levels.3: Ethical conduct standards and anti-corruption controls are implemented and generally effective.
levels.4: Strong ethics programs, whistleblowing mechanisms and anti-corruption controls are actively monitored and enforced.
levels.5: Ethical leadership and anti-corruption practices are deeply embedded in organizational culture and recognized as leading practice within the sector.

criteria.name: Our organisation conducts materiality assessment and integrated material ESG risks and opportunities and link them into strategy, risk management and decision making

levels.0: ESG materiality assessment is not conducted by the organisation, or no ESG considerations are incorporated into management processes.
levels.1: ESG issues are recognized in an ad hoc manner, but no formal materiality assessment is conducted and ESG factors are rarely considered in strategic decisions.
levels.2: A preliminary materiality assessment has been undertaken, and some significant ESG risks and opportunities are identified, but integration into strategy and risk management is limited and inconsistent
levels.3: The organisation conducts periodic materiality assessments and incorporates key ESG risks and opportunities into selected strategic plans, risk registers, and management decisions.
levels.4: Formal and systematic materiality assessments are conducted using stakeholder input and evidence-based analysis. Material ESG issues are consistently integrated into corporate strategy, enterprise risk management, capital allocation, and operational decision-making.
levels.5: Materiality assessment is fully embedded in governance and strategic planning. Dynamic ESG risk and opportunity analysis informs all major decisions, performance targets, innovation, and long-term value creation, with benchmarking against recognized leading practices and continuous improvement.

criteria.name: HR processes are digitized through HRIS platforms.

levels.0: No HRIS exists; all HR processes are manual (paper files, spreadsheets).
levels.1: Basic HRIS used only for employee database and payroll; <20% of HR processes digitized
levels.2: HRIS covers core processes (recruitment, leave, attendance) for 20–40% of modules; some manual workarounds remain.
levels.3: 40–70% of HR processes digitized (e.g., onboarding, performance, offboarding); integration between modules limited.
levels.4: 70–90% of HR processes digitized and integrated (core HR, talent, time, payroll); minimal manual intervention.
levels.5: >90% of HR processes fully digitized and automated; HRIS integrates with finance, IT, and operations; mobile access for all employees.

criteria.name: Data analytics are used in HR decision-making.

levels.0: No HR data analytics capability; no reporting beyond headcount.
levels.1: Basic descriptive reports (e.g., turnover, headcount) generated manually (Excel); used only for compliance.
levels.2: Standardized HR dashboards exist (e.g., turnover, time-to-hire); used quarterly; no predictive or diagnostic analysis.
levels.3: Monthly HR metrics reviewed by leadership; root-cause analysis performed (e.g., exit interview themes linked to turnover).
levels.4: Predictive analytics used (e.g., attrition risk, hiring success probability); data-driven decisions documented (e.g., retention actions).
levels.5: Prescriptive analytics (e.g., 'what if' scenarios) and AI-driven insights; HR analytics integrated with business strategy; dedicated people analytics team.

criteria.name: AI or automation tools support HR operations.

levels.0: No AI or automation in HR.
levels.1: Basic automation for 1–2 repetitive tasks (e.g., auto-email reminders); no AI.
levels.2: Rule-based RPA (robotic process automation) for payroll data entry or onboarding docs; <10% of HR tasks automated
levels.3: AI used in one area (e.g., resume screening, chatbot for FAQs); 10–30% of HR tasks automated.
levels.4: Multiple AI tools (e.g., candidate matching, sentiment analysis, learning recommendations); 30–60% of HR tasks automated.
levels.5: AI integrated across talent lifecycle (sourcing, assessment, development, retention); >60% of HR tasks automated; continuous learning AI models.

criteria.name: Employees receive digital skills training.

levels.0: No digital skills training offered.
levels.1: <10% of employees complete basic digital literacy training (e.g., MS Office) annually.
levels.2: 10–30% of employees complete role-specific digital training (e.g., CRM, collaboration tools).
levels.3: 30–60% of employees complete digital skills training annually; curriculum includes data literacy, automation basics.
levels.4: 60–80% of employees complete training; personalized learning paths based on digital skill gaps; certification options.
levels.5: >80% of employees complete advanced digital training (e.g., AI literacy, low-code, data analytics); digital skills tied to career progression; external benchmark (e.g., Digital Skills Award).

criteria.name: The organization supports innovation and experimentation.

levels.0: No innovation program or experimentation culture.
levels.1: Innovation mentioned in values but no budget, time, or process; risk aversion high.
levels.2: Occasional hackathons or idea boxes; <10% of employees participate; no funding for experiments.
levels.3: Formal innovation program (e.g., innovation challenges, small pilot budget); 10–30% employee participation; 'fail fast' tolerated in low-risk areas.
levels.4: Dedicated innovation budget and time (e.g., 5% time); 30–60% participation; experiments tracked in portfolio; successes scaled.
levels.5: Innovation KPIs (e.g., % revenue from new ideas, experiment success rate); psychological safety scores high; external innovation recognition.

criteria.name: Digital collaboration tools are effectively utilized.

levels.0: No digital collaboration tools (e.g., no Teams, Slack, Zoom, SharePoint).
levels.1: Tools exist but <20% of employees use them regularly; heavy reliance on email.
levels.2: 20–40% of employees use collaboration tools; basic usage (e.g., chat, file sharing).
levels.3: 40–70% adoption; tools used for meetings, document co-authoring, project tracking; governance exists.
levels.4: 70–90% adoption; integrated with workflows (e.g., approvals, task assignments); collaboration metrics tracked (e.g., response time).
levels.5: >90% adoption; AI-enhanced collaboration (e.g., meeting summaries, automated workflows); employee satisfaction >85%; benchmarking against digital-first organizations.

criteria.name: Cybersecurity awareness training exists.

levels.0: No cybersecurity awareness training.
levels.1: <20% of employees complete basic security training (e.g., password hygiene) annually.
levels.2: 20–50% complete annual training; compliance-based only.
levels.3: 50–80% complete training; includes phishing simulations quarterly.
levels.4: 80–95% complete training; role-specific modules (e.g., finance, HR); click-through rates <10% in phishing tests.
levels.5: >95% completion; continuous micro-learning; gamification; measured reduction in security incidents (>50% year-on-year).

criteria.name: Workforce digital readiness is assessed.

levels.0: No digital readiness assessment.
levels.1: Informal manager observation only; no structured assessment.
levels.2: Self-assessment survey conducted once; no action planning.
levels.3: Annual digital skills assessment (self or manager-rated) for 30–60% of workforce; results aggregated.
levels.4: Assessment for 60–90% of workforce; includes technical and behavioral digital competencies; gap analysis drives training.
levels.5: Continuous assessment (e.g., project-based evaluation, digital footprints); predictive readiness scores; individual development plans linked to results.

criteria.name: Employee self-service systems exist.

levels.0: No employee self-service (ESS) portal.
levels.1: ESS exists but <20% of employees use it; only view-only access (e.g., pay stubs).
levels.2: 20–50% of employees use ESS for basic transactions (e.g., leave requests, address changes).
levels.3: 50–80% use ESS for multiple functions (e.g., benefits enrollment, time tracking, training registration).
levels.4: 80–95% use ESS; mobile app available; employees can update personal data, access payslips, request approvals.
levels.5: >95% use ESS; AI chatbot for HR queries; employees can initiate promotions, transfers, or manager changes via workflow; zero paper HR forms.

criteria.name: HR innovation outcomes are measured.

levels.0: No HR innovation metrics tracked.
levels.1: Informal tracking only; no defined innovation KPIs for HR.
levels.2: Basic metrics tracked (e.g., number of ideas submitted); no outcome measurement.
levels.3: Innovation outcomes measured periodically (e.g., process improvements, cost savings from HR tech).
levels.4: Systematic measurement of HR innovation impact on business outcomes; regular reporting to leadership.
levels.5: Advanced analytics linking HR innovation to organizational performance; continuous improvement framework; external benchmarking and recognition.

criteria.name: Our organization has a comprehensive HIV/AIDS/NCD workplace policy,

levels.0: No HIV/AIDS/NCD workplace policy exists.
levels.1: HIV/AIDS/NCD issues are addressed informally with no documented policy framework.
levels.2: A basic HIV/AIDS/NCD policy exists but lacks comprehensiveness or effective implementation.
levels.3: A formal HIV/AIDS/NCD workplace policy exists and is communicated to employees.
levels.4: The policy is comprehensive, regularly reviewed and integrated into HR and wellness practices.
levels.5: The organization demonstrates leading practice through a comprehensive, well-implemented and continuously improved HIV/AIDS/NCD workplace policy aligned with national and international standards.

criteria.name: Employees have been sensitized and trained on HIV/AIDS/NCD and reproductive health issues, including workplace rights, responsibilities, prevention, and support mechanisms.

levels.0: No sensitization or training is conducted.
levels.1: Awareness activities are rare and reach few employees.
levels.2: Basic sensitization programs are conducted occasionally, but coverage is inconsistent.
levels.3: Regular HIV/AIDS/NCD and reproductive health awareness training is provided to most employees.
levels.4: Comprehensive and structured training programs are implemented organization-wide with high participation levels.
levels.5: Continuous, inclusive and impactful education programmes are embedded in organizational culture, promoting awareness, prevention and non-discrimination

criteria.name: Our organization provides or facilitates access to HIV/AIDS/NCD prevention initiatives, testing, counseling, treatment, and related clinical services for employees and their dependents.

levels.0: No HIV/AIDS/NCD-related support services are available.
levels.1: Limited support exists and access to services is difficult or inconsistent.
levels.2: Some prevention or referral services are available but with limited employee coverage.
levels.3: The organization facilitates access to HIV/AIDS/NCD prevention, testing and counseling services for employees.
levels.4: Comprehensive support services including treatment referrals and wellness support are accessible to employees and dependents.
levels.5: The organization provides or partners to deliver integrated, accessible and high-quality HIV/AIDS/NCD healthcare and support services with strong employee utilization and trust.

criteria.name: Our organization actively involves employees in workplace HIV/AIDS/NCD responses

levels.0: Employees are not involved in HIV/AIDS/NCD initiatives.
levels.1: Employee involvement is minimal and largely management-driven.
levels.2: Some employees participate in awareness activities or committees.
levels.3: Employees are moderately involved through peer educators, committees or awareness campaigns.
levels.4: Employee participation is active and supported through structured engagement mechanisms.
levels.5: Employees play a leading role in designing, implementing and championing workplace HIV/AIDS/NCD programmes and awareness initiatives.

criteria.name: Our organization equips managers and supervisors with the skills to appropriately address HIV/AIDS/NCD-related issues and concerns in the workplace.

levels.0: Managers receive no training on HIV/AIDS/NCD workplace issues.
levels.1: Managers have limited awareness and lack confidence in handling HIV/AIDS/NCD-related matters.
levels.2: Some managers receive basic sensitization training.
levels.3: Managers are periodically trained on HIV/AIDS/NCD workplace rights, support and confidentiality issues.
levels.4: Most managers are equipped to effectively address HIV/AIDS/NCD-related workplace concerns and support employees appropriately.
levels.5: Leadership capability on HIV/AIDS/NCD management is highly developed, with managers consistently demonstrating empathy, compliance and supportive leadership practices.

criteria.name: Our organization offers HIV/AIDS/NCD support and wellness programmes for employees and, where applicable, their families (spouses/partners and children).

levels.0: No HIV/AIDS/NCD support or wellness programmes exist.
levels.1: Limited support initiatives exist with low accessibility or awareness.
levels.2: Basic wellness programmes are available but coverage is limited.
levels.3: Structured HIV/AIDS/NCD support and wellness programmes are available to employees.
levels.4: Comprehensive wellness programmes extend to families and include counseling, support and awareness services.
levels.5: Holistic HIV/AIDS/NCD wellness programmes are fully integrated into employee wellbeing strategies and are recognized as best practice within the sector.

criteria.name: Our organization allocates adequate financial, human, and logistical resources to ensure HIV/AIDS/NCD programmes are implemented effectively and sustainably.

levels.0: No resources are allocated to HIV/AIDS/NCD programmes.
levels.1: Resources are inadequate and programmes are poorly supported.
levels.2: Some resources are allocated, but implementation capacity remains limited.
levels.3: Adequate resources are allocated to support key HIV/AIDS/NCD activities and programmes.
levels.4: Dedicated budgets, personnel and logistical support ensure consistent programme implementation.
levels.5: HIV/AIDS/NCD programmes are sustainably resourced, strategically prioritized and continuously strengthened through long-term investment and partnerships.

criteria.name: Our organization formally monitors, evaluates, and reviews the effectiveness and impact of workplace HIV/AIDS/NCD programmes and initiatives.

levels.0: No monitoring or evaluation of HIV/AIDS/NCD programmes exists.
levels.1: Monitoring is informal and inconsistent.
levels.2: Some programme reviews occur, but data collection and analysis are limited.
levels.3: HIV/AIDS/NCD programme performance is periodically monitored and reviewed using defined indicators.
levels.4: Monitoring and evaluation systems are structured, data-driven and support programme improvement.
levels.5: Advanced monitoring, evaluation and learning systems are embedded, demonstrating measurable programme impact and continuous improvement.

criteria.name: Our organization participates in HIV/AIDS/NCD-related community outreach, awareness, or support programmes as part of its corporate social responsibility initiatives.

levels.0: No community HIV/AIDS/NCD outreach or CSR involvement exists.
levels.1: Community support activities are rare or symbolic.
levels.2: The organization occasionally participates in HIV/AIDS/NCD awareness or support initiatives.
levels.3: Structured HIV/AIDS/NCD community outreach programmes are implemented periodically.
levels.4: The organization actively supports community HIV/AIDS/NCD initiatives through partnerships, awareness and resource contributions.
levels.5: The organization demonstrates sector leadership in HIV/AIDS/NCD community engagement and social impact through sustained, innovative and collaborative CSR programmes.

criteria.name: Occupational health and safety policies are implemented.

levels.0: No occupational health and safety (OHS) policies .
levels.1: OHS policies are outdated, or poorly communicated.
levels.2: Basic OHS policies exist but implementation is inconsistent.
levels.3: OHS policies are implemented across most departments with periodic monitoring.
levels.4: OHS policies are fully implemented, regularly reviewed, and compliance is monitored.
levels.5: OHS management is proactive, continuously improved, benchmarked against best practice, and embedded in organizational culture.

criteria.name: Workplace incidents are monitored and addressed.

levels.0: Incident monitoring is not done at all.
levels.1: Incidents are rarely documented or addressed.
levels.2: Some incidents are recorded, but follow-up actions are inconsistent.
levels.3: Incident reporting and corrective actions are implemented for most cases.
levels.4: Comprehensive incident monitoring, investigation, and corrective action systems are in place.
levels.5: Real-time monitoring, trend analysis, preventive action, and continuous improvement systems are embedded organization-wide.

criteria.name: Employees receive regular safety training.

levels.0: Safety training is not conducted
levels.1: Little safety training is provided.
levels.2: Safety training is conducted occasionally for limited staff.
levels.3: Regular safety training is provided to most employees.
levels.4: Comprehensive and role-specific safety training is conducted consistently and tracked.
levels.5: Continuous, innovative, and scenario-based safety learning is embedded into employee development and culture.

criteria.name: Anti-harassment policies are enforced.

levels.0: Anti-harassment measures are not in place.
levels.1: No formal anti-harassment policy or enforcement exists.
levels.2: Policies exist but enforcement mechanisms are weak or inconsistent.
levels.3: Anti-harassment policies are communicated and generally enforced.
levels.4: Policies are strongly enforced with clear reporting and disciplinary procedures.
levels.5: Organization demonstrates zero-tolerance culture, high trust, proactive awareness programs, and regular policy reviews.

criteria.name: Whistleblowing mechanisms exist and are trusted.

levels.0: Whistleblowing mechanisms are not available .
levels.1: No formal whistleblowing mechanism exists.
levels.2: Basic reporting channels exist but employees have low trust in them.
levels.3: Reporting mechanisms are functional and confidentiality is moderately assured.
levels.4: Secure, confidential, and well-communicated whistleblowing systems are widely trusted.
levels.5: Independent, transparent, and highly trusted whistleblowing systems drive ethical accountability and continuous improvement.

criteria.name: Ethical breaches are investigated appropriately.

levels.0: Ethical investigations are not conducted.
levels.1: Ethical breaches are rarely investigated or handled inconsistently.
levels.2: Investigations occur occasionally but lack structure or timeliness.
levels.3: Ethical breaches are investigated using standard procedures in most cases.
levels.4: Investigations are timely, fair, documented, and corrective actions are implemented.
levels.5: Robust ethics governance ensures transparent, independent, and preventive investigation practices aligned with global best standards.

criteria.name: Emergency preparedness plans exist

levels.0: Emergency preparedness is not done.
levels.1: No emergency preparedness plans exist.
levels.2: Basic emergency procedures exist but are incomplete or untested.
levels.3: Emergency preparedness plans are documented and occasionally tested.
levels.4: Comprehensive emergency plans are regularly updated, communicated, and tested through drills.
levels.5: Advanced preparedness systems, simulations, business continuity integration, and continuous improvement practices are fully embedded.
